Tensors II:
Universality

The last article dealt with the tensor product construction , now it's time to see what this construction is good for, and how to use only what we care about the construction and forget about the unimportant details. We then extend the theory to larger multilinear maps f:V1⊗…⊗Vk→Yf: V_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes V_k \to Yf:V1​⊗…⊗Vk​→Y.

Universality of the Tensor Product

Strictly speaking, the tensor product of V,WV,WV,W is a 2-tuple (U,u∈Bil(V×W,U))(U, u \in \text{Bil}(V \times W, U))(U,u∈Bil(V×W,U)) such that ∀Y,f∈Bil(V×W,Y),!∃Tf∈Hom(U,Y)∣Tf∘u=f\forall Y,f \in \text{Bil}(V \times W, Y), !\exists T_f \in \text{Hom}(U, Y)\mid T_f \circ u = f∀Y,f∈Bil(V×W,Y),!∃Tf​∈Hom(U,Y)∣Tf​∘u=fWe will call this the universal property of the tensor product. Our U=V⊗W:=F(V×W)/SU = V \otimes W := F^{(V \times W)} / SU=V⊗W:=F(V×W)/S, with u=⊗:=v,w↦[εv,w]u = \otimes := v,w \mapsto [\varepsilon_{v,w}]u=⊗:=v,w↦[εv,w​] is technically just one example of (U,u)(U,u)(U,u) which satisfies the UP. We say
"(U,u)(U, u)(U,u) where u∈Bil(V×W,U)u \in \text{Bil}(V \times W, U)u∈Bil(V×W,U) satisfies the universal property for bilinear maps IFF all bilinear maps from V×W→YV \times W \to YV×W→Y factor uniquely through uuu to a unique linear map U→YU \to YU→Y."

The opposite implication of the above theorem is true as well.

A nice identification

Alright, the actual reason for demanding universal morphisms for bilinear maps be bilinear is a bit deeper, but actually simpler. I just wanted to motivate it in a different direction by showing even non bilinear "common" maps have a bilinear "component" with respect to the direct sum. The actual reason is given by the following claim
∃(U,u) universal   ⟺  Bil(V×W,Y)≅Hom(U,Y) naturally \exists (U, u) \text{ universal } \iff \text{Bil}(V \times W, Y) \cong \text{Hom}(U, Y) \text{ naturally }∃(U,u) universal ⟺Bil(V×W,Y)≅Hom(U,Y) naturally  That is, universal morphisms for bilinear maps, which themselves are bilinear by definition, imply and are implied by the equivalency between bilinear maps and linear ones on UUU. Thus we care way more about unversal morphisms than common ones so that we can simultaneously show this identification. As well, the term "naturally" means the isomorphisms respect linear morphisms between any two X,YX,YX,Y in the following sense: if ηX:Bil(V×W,X)→Hom(U,X)\eta_{X}: \text{Bil}(V \times W, X) \to \text{Hom}(U, X)ηX​:Bil(V×W,X)→Hom(U,X) and ηY:Bil(V×W,Y)→Hom(U,Y)\eta_Y: \text{Bil}(V \times W, Y) \to \text{Hom}(U, Y)ηY​:Bil(V×W,Y)→Hom(U,Y) are both isomorphisms, then the family {η−}\{\eta_{-}\}{η−​} is called natural if for any l∈Hom(X,Y)l \in \text{Hom}( X, Y)l∈Hom(X,Y) we have ηY(l∘p)=l∘ηX(p)\eta_Y(l \circ p) = l \circ \eta_{X}(p)ηY​(l∘p)=l∘ηX​(p) for all p∈Bil(V×W,X)p \in \text{Bil}(V \times W, X)p∈Bil(V×W,X)

Surjectivity follows since given any linear fff, f∘uf \circ uf∘u is bilinear. So universal bilinear maps are a way to construct a natural isomorphism between bilinear maps and homomorphisms, and vice-versa. One might further ask, since we can pick different constructions for universal maps, just how "different" are two universal (U,u)(U,u)(U,u)? Not very.
Universal bilinear pairs (U,u)(U,u)(U,u) are unique up to unique isomorphism.
That is, if (U,u)(U, u)(U,u) and (U~,u~)(\tilde{U}, \tilde{u})(U~,u~) are both universal pairs for bilinear maps, then there is a unique isomorphism ζ:U→U~\zeta: U \to \tilde{U}ζ:U→U~ such that ζ∘u=u~\zeta \circ u = \tilde{u}ζ∘u=u~

If (U,u)(U, u)(U,u) is a universal pair for bilinear maps, all automorphisms aaa on UUU give new universal morphisms a∘ua \circ ua∘u.
This means, for example (with everything over R\realsR), the autmorphism a:V⊗W→V⊗Wa: V \otimes W \to V \otimes Wa:V⊗W→V⊗W defined by v⊗w↦2v⊗wv \otimes w \mapsto 2 v \otimes wv⊗w↦2v⊗w and linearly extended on V⊗WV \otimes WV⊗W gives a new universal morphism u~(v,w)=2v⊗w\tilde{u}(v, w) = 2 v \otimes wu~(v,w)=2v⊗w. This should be clear, since if fff was the unique linear map composed with ⊗\otimes⊗ to give some bilinear map, using this new univeral morphism means we just need to half fff to get the corresponding morphism. If aaa was more complicated, then we would invert it instead, which we can do since it's an automorphism.

Features and Generalizations

Let's actually forget our free-space-quotient construction of the tensor product and use an arbitrary universal morphism for bilinear maps from now on. Universality is all we'll need to use to further investigate the tensor product; plus, since (U,u)(U, u)(U,u) is unique up to unique isomorphism, all constructions are unique up to isomorphism anyway. We need to redefine our notation; let (U,u)(U, u)(U,u) be universal for bilinear maps over V×WV \times WV×W, and define V⊗W:=Uv⊗w:=u(v,w)V \otimes W := U \\ v \otimes w := u(v, w)V⊗W:=Uv⊗w:=u(v,w) That is, we are divorcing ⊗\otimes⊗ from the free-space-quotient construction. We can then say
"(V⊗W,(v,w)↦v⊗w)(V \otimes W, (v,w) \mapsto v \otimes w)(V⊗W,(v,w)↦v⊗w) is the unique (up to unique isomorphism) universal pair for bilinear maps."
We now show a very important statement, that universal bilinear maps generate universal multilinear maps of higher degree. Firstly, since the domain for multilinear maps can now be an arbitrary number of spaces V1…VnV_1 \ldots V_nV1​…Vn​ we need a way to denote them. We will call the [up to unique isomorphism] universal multilinear pair (M,m)[V1…Vk]=(M[V1…Vk],m[V1…Vk])(M, m)[V_1 \ldots V_k] = (M[V_1 \ldots V_k], m[V_1 \ldots V_k])(M,m)[V1​…Vk​]=(M[V1​…Vk​],m[V1​…Vk​]) which is taken to be universal for multilinear maps over V1…VkV_1 \ldots V_kV1​…Vk​ - the first object being the vector space and the second being the universal morphism. This pair is unique up to unique isomorphism for V1…VkV_1 \ldots V_kV1​…Vk​. We will use the special notation (B,b)[V1,V2]=(B[V1,V2],b[V1,V2])=(M[V1,V2],m[V1,V2])(B,b)[V_1, V_2] = (B[V_1,V_2], b[V_1, V_2]) = (M[V_1,V_2], m[V_1, V_2])(B,b)[V1​,V2​]=(B[V1​,V2​],b[V1​,V2​])=(M[V1​,V2​],m[V1​,V2​]) for universal bilinear pairs. We will write (M1i,m1i)=(M[V1…Vi],m[V1…Vi])(M_1^i, m_1^i) = (M[V_1 \ldots V_i], m[V_1 \ldots V_i])(M1i​,m1i​)=(M[V1​…Vi​],m[V1​…Vi​]) and use B,bB,bB,b when there are only two spaces in the domain.

It's at this point where it would be wise to see an example to consolidate what we've been discussing. Associativity for example means ϕ:V1×V2×V3→(V1⊗V2)⊗V3v1,v2,v3↦(v1⊗v2)⊗v3\phi: V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3 \to (V_1 \otimes V_2) \otimes V_3 \\ v_1,v_2,v_3 \mapsto (v_1 \otimes v_2) \otimes v_3ϕ:V1​×V2​×V3​→(V1​⊗V2​)⊗V3​v1​,v2​,v3​↦(v1​⊗v2​)⊗v3​ and ψ:V1×V2×V3→V1⊗(V2⊗V3)v1,v2,v3↦v1⊗(v2⊗v3)\psi: V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3 \to V_1 \otimes (V_2 \otimes V_3) \\ v_1,v_2,v_3 \mapsto v_1 \otimes (v_2 \otimes v_3)ψ:V1​×V2​×V3​→V1​⊗(V2​⊗V3​)v1​,v2​,v3​↦v1​⊗(v2​⊗v3​) are unique up to unique isomorphism, and both morphisms are universal for trilinear functions on V1×V2×V3V_1 \times V_2 \times V_3V1​×V2​×V3​. Thus nnn-repeated use of ⊗\otimes⊗ is taken to denote the\text{\it the}the (up to unique isomorphism) universal map or space for nnn-linear maps and for example we can write ω\omegaω as ω(v1…v5)=v1⊗…⊗v5\omega(v_1 \ldots v_5) = v_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes v_5ω(v1​…v5​)=v1​⊗…⊗v5​

The Multilinear Generalization (and a bit of practical exposition)

I could end the article here, but there's a consequence of our construction that needs addressing. Let's say you have 5 spaces V1…V5V_1 \ldots V_5V1​…V5​ and a universal morphism ϕ\phiϕ for 555-linear maps over their product, something like ϕ:v1…v5↦(v1⊗(v2⊗(v3⊗v4)))⊗v5\phi: v_1 \ldots v_5 \mapsto (v_1 \otimes (v_2 \otimes (v_3 \otimes v_4))) \otimes v_5 \\ϕ:v1​…v5​↦(v1​⊗(v2​⊗(v3​⊗v4​)))⊗v5​ This requires 4 separate applications of the universal bilinear map, and is an O(4)O(4)O(4) operation. That's all fine and well, but what if you discover that the ViV_iVi​ are actually M[Wai…Wbi]M[W_{a_i} \ldots W_{b_i}]M[Wai​​…Wbi​​] universal spaces over Wai…WbiW_{a_i} \ldots W_{b_i}Wai​​…Wbi​​ with universal morphism pi=m[Wai…Wbi]p_i = m[W_{a_i} \ldots W_{b_i}]pi​=m[Wai​​…Wbi​​] and you know that vi=pi(wai…wbi)v_i = p_i(w_{a_i} \ldots w_{b_i})vi​=pi​(wai​​…wbi​​). After substitution, you ask yourself, "do I get a ccc-linear morphism over the WWW spaces, where c=∑ci=∑(bi−ai+1)c = \sum c_i = \sum (b_i - a_i + 1)c=∑ci​=∑(bi​−ai​+1)?" Let's make this concrete, suppose V1=M[W1,W2]V2=M[W3,W4,W5]V3=M[W6,W7]V4=M[W8,W9,W10]V5=M[W11,W12]\begin{align*} V_1 &= M[W_1, W_2] \\ V_2 &= M[W_3,W_4,W_5] \\ V_3 &= M[W_6, W_7] \\ V_4 &= M[W_8, W_9, W_{10}]\\ V_5 &= M[W_{11}, W_{12}] \end{align*}V1​V2​V3​V4​V5​​=M[W1​,W2​]=M[W3​,W4​,W5​]=M[W6​,W7​]=M[W8​,W9​,W10​]=M[W11​,W12​]​ We can absolutely derive the ccc-linear morphism; simply start with the inner parentheses and move outward. We know V3⊗V4=M[W6…W10]v3⊗v4=p3(w6,w7)⊗p4(w8,w9,w10)=m[W6,W7](w6,w7)⊗m[W8,W9,W10](w8,w9,w10)=m[W6…W10](w6…w10)\begin{align*} V_3 \otimes V_4 = M[W_6 \ldots W_{10}] \\ v_3 \otimes v_4 = p_3(w_6, w_7) \otimes p_4(w_8,w_9,w_{10}) \\= m[W_6, W_7](w_6,w_7) \otimes m[W_8,W_9,W_{10}](w_8,w_9,w_{10}) \\ =m[W_6 \ldots W_{10}](w_6 \ldots w_{10}) \end{align*}V3​⊗V4​=M[W6​…W10​]v3​⊗v4​=p3​(w6​,w7​)⊗p4​(w8​,w9​,w10​)=m[W6​,W7​](w6​,w7​)⊗m[W8​,W9​,W10​](w8​,w9​,w10​)=m[W6​…W10​](w6​…w10​)​ by our theorem, since ⊗\otimes⊗ is the bilinear universal. We would like to not have to execute this procedure to prove similar claims each time. What if instead of ϕ\phiϕ being over V1×…×V5V_1 \times \ldots \times V_5V1​×…×V5​ it was over V1×…×V200,000,000V_1 \times \ldots \times V_{200,000,000}V1​×…×V200,000,000​? We solve this issue with the following theorem.
Mutlilinear universal maps generate multilinear universal maps with degree equal to the sum of the degrees of the component maps. That is, if (Pi,pi)=(M[Vai…Vbi],m[Vai…Vbi])(P_i, p_i) = (M[V_{a_i} \ldots V_{b_i}], m[V_{a_i} \ldots V_{b_i}])(Pi​,pi​)=(M[Vai​​…Vbi​​],m[Vai​​…Vbi​​]) are universal pairs for cic_ici​-linear maps over Vai…VbiV_{a_i} \ldots V_{b_i}Vai​​…Vbi​​ for i=1…ni = 1 \ldots ni=1…n, where ci=bi−ai+1c_i = b_i-a_i+1ci​=bi​−ai​+1, and if (P,p)=(M[P1…Pn],m[P1…Pn])(P, p) = (M[P_1 \ldots P_n], m[P_1 \ldots P_n])(P,p)=(M[P1​…Pn​],m[P1​…Pn​]) is a universal pair for nnn-linear functions over ∏i=1nPi\prod_{i=1}^n P_i∏i=1n​Pi​, then (P,p(p1(−)…pn(−)))(P, p(p_1(-) \ldots p_n(-)))(P,p(p1​(−)…pn​(−))) is the unique (up to unique isomorphism) universal pair for ccc-linear functions over Va1…VbnV_{a_1} \ldots V_{b_n}Va1​​…Vbn​​, where c=∑cic = \sum c_ic=∑ci​.

Thus X=(B[P~,Pn],b[P~,Pn](p~(p1(−)…pn−1(−)),pn(−)))X = (B[\tilde{P}, P_n], b[\tilde{P}, P_n](\tilde{p}(p_1(-) \ldots p_{n-1}(-)), p_n(-)))X=(B[P~,Pn​],b[P~,Pn​](p~​(p1​(−)…pn−1​(−)),pn​(−))) is unversal over Va1…VbnV_{a_1} \ldots V_{b_n}Va1​​…Vbn​​. I hope that wasn't too hairy; the proof isn't particularly complicated it's just that there are alot of different variables everywhere. But the utility should not be lost on the reader.
